- SPV mergers deliver governance optics, not P&L — don't model cost savings.
- 30-36 month project timelines = structurally slower capitalization conversion than bull-case assumes.
- GIB (Great Indian Bustard) Supreme Court ruling: NO impact on PG's Rajasthan/Ramgarh/Bhadla projects (all outside GIB zone) — removes an overhang.

bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Regulatory tariff-reset risk — The bulk of revenue is earned under the Regulated Tariff Mechanism, where transmission charges (Return on Equity, depreciation, O&M recovery, interest on working capital) are set by CERC-notified regulations that reset periodically; the new CERC (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024 for the 2024-29 tariff block reduced the base Return on Equity for assets commissioned on or after 1 April 2024 to 15.0% (pre-tax gross-up) versus 15.5% protected for pre-2024 assets, showing that future tariff-block resets can directly move realised returns.
- Revenue concentration in transmission — Transmission and transmission-related activities constituted 85.14% of total income in FY26, leaving the Company's results highly dependent on the regulatory and demand dynamics of a single core business line despite diversification efforts in telecom, consultancy and new energy verticals.
- Regulatory/licensing non-approval risk on specific assets — CERC has, in the past, withdrawn regulatory approval for a transmission project element: for POWERGRID Vemagiri Transmission Limited, CERC's order dated 6 April 2015 held that the Vemagiri-Khammam-Hyderabad 765kV D/C lines were neither required as an evacuation line nor a system-strengthening line and withdrew the licence/regulatory approval for that transmission project, illustrating exposure to regulator determinations that can strand or invalidate specific project revenue.
- Broad multi-domain enterprise risk exposure — Management's own Enterprise Risk Management framework spans strategic, operational, financial, HR, compliance, sustainability and information/cyber-security risk domains across the organisation, reviewed by a Board-level Risk Management Committee (convened three times in FY26) and a Chief Risk Officer, indicating risk is broad-based rather than confined to a single identifiable driver.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: During FY26 the Company added nine substations, taking its total to 291, with key additions at Bhadla, Ramgarh and Dausa (Rajasthan) to evacuate power from renewable-energy-rich areas, and commissioning of the KPS-2 and KPS-3 substations tied to the Khavda Renewable Energy Evacuation System in Gujarat. Several green-energy evacuation corridors were also commissioned, including Bhadla-Sikar, Ahmedabad-Lakadia and Ahmedabad-Navsari. India's first indigenously manufactured 400kV insulated cross-arm was developed and deployed to ease Right-of-Way constraints on new lines. POWERGRID Bellary Davanagere Transmission Limited (PBDTL), acquired via TBCB on 12 February 2026, is implementing transmission-system strengthening to integrate additional renewable capacity at Davanagere (0.25 GW) and Bellary (2.75 GW), with a CERC transmission licence application pending. Through wholly owned subsidiary PowerTel, the Company is expanding into Data Centre services: a commercial Data Centre at the POWERGRID Manesar Substation (Haryana) is under implementation, and land has been acquired in Chennai for a Zone-2 Data Centre. During the year the Company secured nine TBCB transmission projects and its first-ever Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project in Andhra Pradesh. For FY27, several renewable-energy evacuation projects are slated for completion, including substations at Kopal, Gadag, Vataman, Kurnool-III and Ananthpuram with their associated transmission networks, against a stated FY27 capex target of approximately Rs 37,000 crore and a capitalisation target of approximately Rs 30,000 crore. On the technology/R&D side, the Company commissioned a 400kV, 315 MVA synthetic ester oil-filled transformer (Asia's first) for improved environmental safety, launched a programme to develop domestic suppliers for high-voltage Emergency Restoration System (ERS) components up to 400kV that were previously imported, and established a POWERGRID Centre of Excellence in Cyber Security at a premier institute for R&D on Operational Technology security in transmission and grid operations.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's per-capita electricity consumption is expected to rise from about 1,541 kWh in 2024 to around 2,000 kWh by 2030, over 4,000 kWh by 2047, and 7,000-10,000 kWh by 2070, necessitating sustained power infrastructure development.
- Energy demand is expected to grow at the fastest rate among major economies, driven by urbanisation, industrialisation, electric mobility, energy-intensive technologies, digital infrastructure and green hydrogen production.
- Per the Mid-Term Review of the 20th Electric Power Survey, peak electricity demand is projected to rise from 289 GW (2026-27) to 345 GW (2029-30) and further to 388 GW (2031-32); the country has already seen new all-time peak demand records since April 2026, reaching 270.8 GW on May 21, 2026.
- Data Centres and Green Hydrogen are emerging as new large demand centres -- AI-led data-centre clusters are coming up as large concentrated point loads, while green hydrogen is expected to add approximately 71 GW of demand by 2032; India's data-centre capacity of around 1,280 MW is projected to expand four to five times by 2030.
- India's power sector is on a multi-decade investment cycle in which transmission has evolved into a platform empowering the energy transition, underpinned by the Central Electricity Authority's plan to integrate over 900 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2035-36.
- Development of about 76 GW of hydropower capacity across 12 sub-basins of the Brahmaputra is viewed as another major driver of transmission expansion.
- Grid-scale battery energy storage is becoming central to grid utilisation, with cumulative BESS capacity rising sharply and industry estimates placing India's cumulative storage requirement at about 888 GWh by 2035-36, requiring close integration with the transmission network.
- Cross-border power transfer capacity with neighbouring countries is expected to rise from about 10 GW currently to about 26 GW going forward, supporting regional power exchange.
- A large and growing portfolio of Regulated Tariff Mechanism (RTM) assets continues to provide regulatory stability alongside the Company's competitively bid (TBCB) project leadership.
- Works in hand of approximately ₹1.7 lakh crore, including CWIP of ₹0.48 lakh crore, together with a bidding pipeline in excess of ₹1.1 lakh crore, provide strong multi-year execution visibility.
- The wider Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) sector opportunity per CTUIL's Rolling Plan 2030-31 comprises 77,228 ckm of transmission lines and 6,97,747 MVA of transformation capacity at an estimated cost of ₹5,41,481 crore over the next five years, of which ~42,000 ckm/414 GVA (~₹2.83 lakh crore) is under construction and ~34,400 ckm/284 GVA (~₹2.58 lakh crore) is under planning/approval/bidding.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's per-capita electricity consumption is expected to rise from about 1,541 kWh in 2024 to around 2,000 kWh by 2030, over 4,000 kWh by 2047, and 7,000-10,000 kWh by 2070, necessitating sustained power infrastructure development.
- Energy demand is expected to grow at the fastest rate among major economies, driven by urbanisation, industrialisation, electric mobility, energy-intensive technologies, digital infrastructure and green hydrogen production.
- Per the Mid-Term Review of the 20th Electric Power Survey, peak electricity demand is projected to rise from 289 GW (2026-27) to 345 GW (2029-30) and further to 388 GW (2031-32); the country has already seen new all-time peak demand records since April 2026, reaching 270.8 GW on May 21, 2026.
- Data Centres and Green Hydrogen are emerging as new large demand centres -- AI-led data-centre clusters are coming up as large concentrated point loads, while green hydrogen is expected to add approximately 71 GW of demand by 2032; India's data-centre capacity of around 1,280 MW is projected to expand four to five times by 2030.
- India's power sector is on a multi-decade investment cycle in which transmission has evolved into a platform empowering the energy transition, underpinned by the Central Electricity Authority's plan to integrate over 900 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2035-36.
- Development of about 76 GW of hydropower capacity across 12 sub-basins of the Brahmaputra is viewed as another major driver of transmission expansion.
- Grid-scale battery energy storage is becoming central to grid utilisation, with cumulative BESS capacity rising sharply and industry estimates placing India's cumulative storage requirement at about 888 GWh by 2035-36, requiring close integration with the transmission network.
- Cross-border power transfer capacity with neighbouring countries is expected to rise from about 10 GW currently to about 26 GW going forward, supporting regional power exchange.
- A large and growing portfolio of Regulated Tariff Mechanism (RTM) assets continues to provide regulatory stability alongside the Company's competitively bid (TBCB) project leadership.
- Works in hand of approximately ₹1.7 lakh crore, including CWIP of ₹0.48 lakh crore, together with a bidding pipeline in excess of ₹1.1 lakh crore, provide strong multi-year execution visibility.
- The wider Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) sector opportunity per CTUIL's Rolling Plan 2030-31 comprises 77,228 ckm of transmission lines and 6,97,747 MVA of transformation capacity at an estimated cost of ₹5,41,481 crore over the next five years, of which ~42,000 ckm/414 GVA (~₹2.83 lakh crore) is under construction and ~34,400 ckm/284 GVA (~₹2.58 lakh crore) is under planning/approval/bidding.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: During FY26 the Company added nine substations, taking its total to 291, with key additions at Bhadla, Ramgarh and Dausa (Rajasthan) to evacuate power from renewable-energy-rich areas, and commissioning of the KPS-2 and KPS-3 substations tied to the Khavda Renewable Energy Evacuation System in Gujarat. Several green-energy evacuation corridors were also commissioned, including Bhadla-Sikar, Ahmedabad-Lakadia and Ahmedabad-Navsari. India's first indigenously manufactured 400kV insulated cross-arm was developed and deployed to ease Right-of-Way constraints on new lines. POWERGRID Bellary Davanagere Transmission Limited (PBDTL), acquired via TBCB on 12 February 2026, is implementing transmission-system strengthening to integrate additional renewable capacity at Davanagere (0.25 GW) and Bellary (2.75 GW), with a CERC transmission licence application pending. Through wholly owned subsidiary PowerTel, the Company is expanding into Data Centre services: a commercial Data Centre at the POWERGRID Manesar Substation (Haryana) is under implementation, and land has been acquired in Chennai for a Zone-2 Data Centre. During the year the Company secured nine TBCB transmission projects and its first-ever Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project in Andhra Pradesh. For FY27, several renewable-energy evacuation projects are slated for completion, including substations at Kopal, Gadag, Vataman, Kurnool-III and Ananthpuram with their associated transmission networks, against a stated FY27 capex target of approximately Rs 37,000 crore and a capitalisation target of approximately Rs 30,000 crore. On the technology/R&D side, the Company commissioned a 400kV, 315 MVA synthetic ester oil-filled transformer (Asia's first) for improved environmental safety, launched a programme to develop domestic suppliers for high-voltage Emergency Restoration System (ERS) components up to 400kV that were previously imported, and established a POWERGRID Centre of Excellence in Cyber Security at a premier institute for R&D on Operational Technology security in transmission and grid operations.

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- Guidance conservatism / no upward FY27-28 revision despite FY26 beat → near-term tendering visibility soft.
- Tendering slowdown beyond 73 GW Rajasthan (now reportedly resolving) — pipeline lumpiness risk.
- RoW remains a "perpetual challenge" despite improved GoI compensation guidelines (rural 30% / semi-urban 45% / urban 60% premium).
- Transformer/reactor supply, skilled manpower — addressed but historically caused delays (recent AC projects took 3-3.5 yrs vs 18-mo bids).
- New project timelines normalized to 30-36 months (vs unrealistic 18-24) → slower per-project capitalization cadence.
- BESS competitive weakness vs smaller players.
- Leadership transition: CMD Tyagi retiring (superannuation).
- Summer FY27 demand ~270-275 GW; possible El Niño / gas / hydro deficit (macro, not company-specific).

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- The FY26 capex/capitalization beat is largely commissioning-timing driven (Navsari-Phadge, Bikaner-III sliding into late March) — lumpy, not run-rate.
- Pang-Kaithal (Leh) ~Rs23-25k cr REMOVED from order book — material de-risking/haircut to the headline pipeline; watch for re-award (AC vs HVDC undecided).
- New Rs7.9 lakh cr CEA plan (FY27-36, released 19-Mar at Bharat Electricity Summit) is incremental to existing ongoing projects, not a replacement — but specifics/awarding timeline unknown ("after some time").
- SPV mergers deliver governance optics, not P&L — don't model cost savings.
- 30-36 month project timelines = structurally slower capitalization conversion than bull-case assumes.
- GIB (Great Indian Bustard) Supreme Court ruling: NO impact on PG's Rajasthan/Ramgarh/Bhadla projects (all outside GIB zone) — removes an overhang.

- 45% institutional ownership.
- Self-funds growth via rising PAT + debt at ~80:20 D:E; no equity dilution signalled.
risks & watch-items:
- Guidance conservatism / no upward FY27-28 revision despite FY26 beat → near-term tendering visibility soft.
- Tendering slowdown beyond 73 GW Rajasthan (now reportedly resolving) — pipeline lumpiness risk.
- RoW remains a "perpetual challenge" despite improved GoI compensation guidelines (rural 30% / semi-urban 45% / urban 60% premium).
- Transformer/reactor supply, skilled manpower — addressed but historically caused delays (recent AC projects took 3-3.5 yrs vs 18-mo bids).
- New project timelines normalized to 30-36 months (vs unrealistic 18-24) → slower per-project capitalization cadence.
- BESS competitive weakness vs smaller players.
- Leadership transition: CMD Tyagi retiring (superannuation).
- Summer FY27 demand ~270-275 GW; possible El Niño / gas / hydro deficit (macro, not company-specific).
management quality / tone: Confident, visionary, "nation-building to 2047" framing; strong on operational metrics and execution-capability narrative. Heavy on opportunity-size (Rs15 lakh cr TAM) but candid on guidance being projects-in-hand only. CFO measured/honest (no cost savings claimed on merger). Retiring CMD's valedictory tone.
non-obvious takeaways:
- The FY26 capex/capitalization beat is largely commissioning-timing driven (Navsari-Phadge, Bikaner-III sliding into late March) — lumpy, not run-rate.
- Pang-Kaithal (Leh) ~Rs23-25k cr REMOVED from order book — material de-risking/haircut to the headline pipeline; watch for re-award (AC vs HVDC undecided).
- New Rs7.9 lakh cr CEA plan (FY27-36, released 19-Mar at Bharat Electricity Summit) is incremental to existing ongoing projects, not a replacement — but specifics/awarding timeline unknown ("after some time").
- SPV mergers deliver governance optics, not P&L — don't model cost savings.
- 30-36 month project timelines = structurally slower capitalization conversion than bull-case assumes.
- GIB (Great Indian Bustard) Supreme Court ruling: NO impact on PG's Rajasthan/Ramgarh/Bhadla projects (all outside GIB zone) — removes an overhang.
